Probability distribution (μX​(B)=P(X∈B))

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Probability and statistics Probability theory
OurBigBook.com Words: 31k Articles: 374
A probability distribution describes how the values of a random variable are allocated among possible outcomes. More precisely, the law of a random variable X assigns each measurable set B the probability
μX​(B)=P(X∈B).
(1)
It is a probability measure on the values of X. The underlying experiment can be more elaborate than the output: different experiments may produce the same probability distribution. The law of a random variable retains the probabilities needed to answer questions about that output. [ref].
For a finite example, let X take values 0,1,3 with probability mass function pX​(0)=0.2, pX​(1)=0.5, pX​(3)=0.3. Its probabilities sum to one. The event 0<X≤1 has probability 0.5, whereas 0≤X≤1 has probability 0.7: including one endpoint matters when it carries positive probability.
For a contrasting random variable Y, choose the probability density function fY​(y)=2y on 0≤y≤1, and zero elsewhere. It integrates to one. Now P(1/4<Y≤3/4)=∫1/43/4​2ydy=1/2, while every single outcome has probability zero. The probability density function can have height fY​(0.8)=1.6: probabilities come from integrals over outcome ranges.
The cumulative distribution function answers all threshold questions for a real random variable, regardless of whether there are jumps or a probability density function. A quantile function reverses the direction of the question: given a cumulative probability level, find a threshold. This connects descriptive summaries to inverse transform sampling, which constructs a chosen probability distribution from a uniform distribution.

Normalization of a probability distribution (∫f(x)dx=1)

Words: 61
Probability distribution OurBigBook.com
A probability distribution assigns total probability one to its sample space. For a nonnegative probability density function this means that its integral over the full domain equals one; for a probability mass function the sum of its masses equals one. A nonnegative integrable function with positive finite integral can be divided by that integral to normalize it. A negative function cannot be a probability density function even if a formal manipulation purports to normalize it.

Mixed probability distribution (μ=αμd​+(1−α)μc​)

Words: 250 Articles: 2
Probability distribution OurBigBook.com
A mixed probability distribution combines a discrete probability distribution with a continuous probability distribution. For example, put probability 1/4 at zero and probability 3/4 into a uniform distribution on (0,1). Its cumulative distribution function is 0 for x<0, 1/4+3x/4 for 0≤x<1, and 1 for x≥1. The jump at zero and the continuous increase both contribute; neither an ordinary probability density function alone nor a probability mass function alone describes the whole law.

Mixture of a point mass and an exponential distribution (L(Y)=pδ−c​+(1−p)Exp(λ))

Words: 87
Mixed probability distribution OurBigBook.com
Let c>0, 0≤p≤1 and λ>0. With probability p, take Y=−c; otherwise draw an exponential distribution of rate λ. This mixed probability distribution has a negative atom and a continuous nonnegative component. Its moments are E[Y]=−pc+(1−p)/λ and E[Y2]=pc2+2(1−p)/λ2. The law of total variance equivalently gives Var(Y)=(1−p)/λ2+p(1−p)(c+1/λ)2.
When p<1, conditioning on Y≥0 selects exactly the exponential component, so P(Y≥t∣Y≥0)=e−λt for t≥0. An ordinary probability density function for the continuous component integrates to 1−p, not one; the missing mass is the atom, not a normalization error.

Uniform distribution with an atom at zero (L(S)=(1−q)δ0​+qUnif(0,r))

Words: 105
Mixed probability distribution OurBigBook.com
For 0≤q≤1 and r>0, this mixed probability distribution has probability mass 1−q at zero and ordinary probability density function q/r on (0,r). That ordinary density integrates to q, not to one; conditioned on S>0, the law is the uniform distribution on (0,r). Its cumulative distribution function is zero for s<0, 1−q+qs/r for 0≤s<r, and one for s≥r.
For each positive integer k, integration gives E[Sk]=qrk/(k+1). Thus the expected value is qr/2 and the variance is qr2/3−q2r2/4. The nonzero atom contributes to normalization even though it contributes zero to positive moments. At q=0, conditioning on positive delay is undefined because the conditioning event has probability zero.

Probability mass (P(X=x))

Words: 48
Probability distribution OurBigBook.com
The probability mass at an outcome x is the probability of its singleton, P(X=x). It equals the jump FX​(x)−FX​(x−) of the cumulative distribution function. For a discrete probability distribution these masses form the probability mass function; a continuous probability distribution gives every individual outcome mass zero. Positive probability mass at a point is distinct from the height of a probability density function.

Heavy-tailed distribution (EeθX=∞(θ>0))

Words: 91 Articles: 1
Probability distribution OurBigBook.com
In the right-tail convention, every positive exponential moment is infinite. This is a tail property, not the assertion that the variance or all power moments must be infinite. A heavy-tailed subexponential distribution has the additional property that a sum's far tail is dominated by one large summand.

Subexponential distribution (heavy-tailed, P(X1​+X2​>x)∼2P(X1​>x))

Words: 49
Heavy-tailed distribution OurBigBook.com
For nonnegative independent and identically distributed random variables with unbounded support, this is the displayed two-summand tail asymptotic. The probability that the maximum exceeds x is 1−F(x)2∼2F(x), so the sum and maximum have asymptotically the same tail. This is the basic single-large-arrival effect relevant to queue overflow. The concentration-theory sub-exponential random variable uses a separate light-tail convention.

Infinite divisibility (probability, μ=μn∗n​for every n≥1)

Words: 68
Probability distribution OurBigBook.com
A probability distribution is infinitely divisible if, for every positive integer n, it is the distribution of a sum of n independent and identically distributed random variables. Their common distribution may depend on n. A normal distribution has this property by dividing its mean and variance by n; a Poisson distribution has it by dividing its rate. The unit-time law of a Lévy process is infinitely divisible because it is the sum of its increments on n equal time intervals.

Predictive distribution

Words: 35
Probability distribution OurBigBook.com
A probability law for a future observation conditional on currently available information. A posterior predictive distribution integrates the observation model over the posterior distribution of unknown parameters; a plug-in predictive law instead fixes an estimate of those parameters.

Non-degenerate probability distribution

Words: 24
Probability distribution OurBigBook.com
A probability distribution is non-degenerate when it is not a point mass. This condition excludes constant limits in limit theorems and in the maximum domain of attraction of a distribution function.

Support of a probability distribution (suppμ={x:μ(U)>0 for every open U∋x})

Words: 56 Articles: 1
Probability distribution OurBigBook.com
For a probability measure on a topological space, its support consists of the points whose every open neighborhood has positive probability. For a continuous effort distribution supported on an interval, every open subinterval of that interval has positive probability.

Effort support

Words: 20
Support of a probability distribution OurBigBook.com
An effort support is the support of a probability distribution used to randomize effort in a contest. The all-pay indifference equation with random entry determines this support together with its distribution function.

Kurtosis (κ=E[(X−EX)4]/Var(X)2)

Words: 725 Articles: 4
Probability distribution OurBigBook.com
For a real random variable X with mean μ=EX, finite positive variance 0<σ2=Var(X)<∞, and finite fourth moment, kurtosis is the fourth central moment divided by the square of the variance:
κ(X)=σ4E[(X−μ)4]​=E[Z4],Z=σX−μ​.
(2)
The standard score Z measures distance from the mean in standard deviations. Its fourth power gives a value ten standard deviations away a weight 104=10000 inside the expected value. Thus a small probability mass far from the mean can strongly affect kurtosis. It is useful for describing the contribution of extreme standard scores, but does not by itself describe the height or shape of a probability density function near its peak.[ref]
The normal distribution has kurtosis 3. A random scale can increase kurtosis even when the conditional distribution is normal. A constant random variable has zero variance, so this ratio is undefined. If the variance is finite and positive but the fourth central moment is infinite, the ratio can be written +∞ in an extended sense; it is not a finite kurtosis. If the variance itself is infinite or the mean is undefined, the displayed normalization is unavailable.

Excess kurtosis (γ2​=κ−3)

Words: 157
Kurtosis OurBigBook.com
Excess kurtosis subtracts 3 from kurtosis, making the normal distribution baseline zero. The non-excess convention is sometimes called raw kurtosis; this still uses a fourth central moment, not the uncentered fourth moment E[X4]. Software may report either kurtosis or excess kurtosis, so the convention must be stated.[ref]
For a standard normal distribution, the moment-generating function of a standard normal variable gives E[Z4]=3, hence excess kurtosis zero. For a continuous uniform distribution on [−3​,3​], the mean is zero, the variance is one, and direct integration gives
κ=23​1​∫−3​3​​z4dz=59​,γ2​=−56​.
(3)
The rare-outlier three-point distribution can instead have kurtosis 100 and excess kurtosis 97 with mean zero and variance one. These are calculated properties of specified probability distributions, rather than a measured statistic.

Rare-outlier three-point distribution (P(X=0)=1−q,P(X=±1)=q/2)

Words: 206
Kurtosis OurBigBook.com
For 0<q≤1, put probability mass 1−q at zero and q/2 at each of −1 and 1. This symmetric probability distribution has mean zero. Its second and fourth moments are both q, because the nonzero outcomes have square and fourth power equal to one:
Var(X)=q,E[X4]=q,κ(X)=q2q​=q1​.
(4)
For q=1/4 the kurtosis is 4; for q=1/100 it is 100. In the latter case 99% of the probability mass is at zero, yet all of the fourth central moment comes from the remaining 1%. The standard score Z=X/q​ takes values 0 and ±q−1/2, with variance one. Each nonzero outcome contributes
2q​(q−1/2)4=2q1​
(5)
to kurtosis. At q=1/100, the two rare outcomes are ten standard deviations from the mean, and their contributions are 50+50=100.

For an infinite sequence of real exchangeable random variables, conditional on its invariant sigma-algebra of an exchangeable sequence, the coordinates are independent and identically distributed. In particular, for Borel sets A0​,…,Ap​,

(7)
Here is the core proof. Let Sm​ denote invariance under permutations of coordinates 0,…,m. Symmetrization as conditional expectation identifies the empirical average of each indicator with its conditional expectation on Sm​. The reverse martingale convergence theorem gives its limit conditional on S. Multiplying the averages sums over all ordered coordinate tuples, including repetitions. Symmetrization of the product itself sums over the distinct tuples. The fraction of repeated tuples is at most (2p+1​)/(m+1), so these bounded averages have the same limit. This proves the displayed factorization. Permutation invariance also makes the individual conditional laws identical. A regular conditional distribution on the real line packages that common law as a random probability measure, giving the equivalent mixture-of-iid formulation.

Events in the tail sigma-algebra are invariant because any finite permutation fixes every sufficiently late coordinate. Conversely, exchangeable invariant events are tail events modulo null sets.
Exchangeable invariant events are tail events modulo null sets

For a real sequence of exchangeable random variables, every event A in its invariant sigma-algebra of an exchangeable sequence agrees almost surely with an event of its tail sigma-algebra. Put F=1A​. Approximate F in L1 by its conditional expectation on the first n+1 coordinates. Swap that block with the next n+1 coordinates. Invariance of A and the law shows that the conditional expectation on the second block is an equally good approximation. It is measurable with respect to the tail after index n. The L1 contraction of conditional expectation then bounds ∥F−E[F∣Gn​]∥1​ by twice the approximation error. The reverse martingale convergence theorem gives F=E[F∣⋂n​Gn​] almost surely. Thresholding the latter at 1/2 supplies the required tail event. Together with the reverse inclusion, the two sigma-algebras have identical probability completions.

Probability distribution OurBigBook.com
The beta distribution is an absolutely continuous probability distribution for a random variable X between zero and one. It can describe uncertainty about a probability, such as an unknown coin's chance of heads. For any real α,β>0, its probability density function is
fX​(x)=B(α,β)xα−1(1−x)β−1​,0<x<1,
(12)
and zero outside [0,1]. The normalizer is the Euler beta function, related to the gamma function by the beta-gamma identity:
B(α,β)=∫01​xα−1(1−x)β−1dx=Γ(α+β)Γ(α)Γ(β)​.
(13)
Thus the probability density function integrates to one. [ref].
The endpoint behavior explains why the restrictions are exactly α,β>0: near zero the probability density function behaves like a constant times xα−1, and near one like a constant times (1−x)β−1. These improper integrals converge for positive parameters, even when the probability density function diverges at zero for α<1 or at one for β<1. There is no probability mass at either endpoint: P(X=0)=P(X=1)=0. A probability density function's height is not a probability; an interval's probability is the area under it.
Some useful examples of the beta distribution are:
  • Beta(1,1) is the uniform distribution on (0,1), with probability density function fX​(x)=1.
  • Beta(2,2) has probability density function fX​(x)=6x(1−x): values near one half are favored, and it is a symmetric probability distribution about one half.
  • Beta(2,5) has probability density function fX​(x)=30x(1−x)4. Its mean is 2/7 and its variance is 10/(49⋅8)=5/196≈0.0255102; most of its area lies toward the lower end.
  • Beta(1/2,1/2) is the arcsine distribution, with probability density function fX​(x)=1/(πx(1−x)​). It favors values near both endpoints despite having mean 1/2; its variance is 1/8.
The arcsine distribution curve is plotted only for 0.001≤x≤0.999; its finite plotted ends do not represent finite endpoint values of the probability density function. Using the inverse sine, the shaded central interval has exact probability P(0.1<X<0.9)=1−4arcsin(0.1​)/π≈0.5903, calculated analytically rather than by treating the cropped curve as normalized.
To separate location from spread, write κ=α+β and m=α/κ. The mean and variance of the beta distribution are
E[X]=m=κα​,Var(X)=κ2(κ+1)αβ​=κ+1m(1−m)​.
(14)
The mean specifies the balance between the parameters; their sum κ controls concentration about that mean. Multiplying both parameters by the same positive number preserves the mean and changes the variance. Larger κ puts more area near m and makes the probability density function taller there; the total area stays one. Small κ allows much greater spread, sometimes favoring the endpoints rather than the mean itself.
For example, keeping mean m=0.3 and taking κ=5,20,80 gives the beta distributions Beta(1.5,3.5), Beta(6,14), and Beta(24,56). Their variances are 0.035, 0.01, and 0.21/81≈0.00259259, respectively. Parameters need not be integers.
The formulas follow from two short moment calculations. Multiplying the probability density function by x or x2 increases the first parameter of the Euler beta function:
E[X]=B(α,β)B(α+1,β)​=κα​,E[X2]=B(α,β)B(α+2,β)​=κ(κ+1)α(α+1)​.
(15)
Apply the Gamma function recurrence to the beta-gamma identity, then subtract (E[X])2 from E[X2] to obtain the variance.
The beta distribution is especially convenient as a prior distribution for the unknown success probability P of Bernoulli trials. The Beta-binomial conjugacy says that h successes and t failures update a prior distribution Beta(α,β) to a posterior distribution Beta(α+h,β+t). For example, suppose a coin has prior distribution Beta(2,2) and we observe eight heads and two tails. Its posterior distribution is then Beta(10,4), with posterior mean 5/7. [ref].

Empirical distribution function (Fn​)

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Cumulative distribution function OurBigBook.com
The empirical distribution function counts the fraction of observations at or below a threshold. For a statistical sample of n≥1 real observations X1​,…,Xn​, define
Fn​(x)=n#{i:Xi​≤x}​=n1​∑i=1n​1{Xi​≤x}​.
(22)
Each indicator function contributes one exactly when its observation is counted. Equivalently, Fn​(x)=Pn​((−∞,x]), where the empirical measure Pn​=n−1∑i​δXi​​ assigns probability mass 1/n to each observation, including repeated observations.[ref]
Choose the illustrative statistical sample [1,1,2,4,6]. Its empirical distribution function is
F5​(x)=⎩⎨⎧​02/53/54/51​x<1,1≤x<2,2≤x<4,4≤x<6,6≤x.​
(23)
For example, F5​(1)=2/5 counts both observations equal to 1, F5​(3)=3/5, and F5​(4)=4/5. There is no observation at 3, so there is no jump there. The five observations produce only four distinct jump locations.
The convention Xi​≤x makes the empirical distribution function right-continuous: once a threshold reaches an observation, that observation remains counted immediately to its right. For a finite statistical sample, the count is constant from any x up to the next larger observed value, proving right continuity. Its left-hand limit Fn​(x−) counts observations strictly below x, so
Fn​(x)−Fn​(x−)=n#{i:Xi​=x}​.
(24)
A value occurring m times causes one jump of size m/n. At 1 the jump is 2/5; at 2, 4, and 6 each jump is 1/5. All jumps sum to one. Thus the empirical distribution function is a nondecreasing step function with limits zero and one, and is itself a valid cumulative distribution function.
This turns many questions about data into simple cumulative distribution function operations. The observed fraction in (a,b] is Fn​(b)−Fn​(a): for (1,4] it is 4/5−2/5=2/5, counting 2 and 4 but excluding both 1s. Including the left endpoint gives Fn​(4)−Fn​(1−)=4/5. A sample quantile reads the same staircase in reverse: the smallest threshold reaching 1/2 is 2. Unlike a histogram, this representation requires no choice of bins; its jumps retain every observation and its multiplicity.
The exact description of a finite statistical sample must be distinguished from a statistical model for how it was obtained. The empirical distribution function is defined for any finite list, with no independence assumption. Once the list is observed, its counts are fixed. For statistical inference, one often models X1​,…,Xn​ as independent and identically distributed random variables with an unknown population cumulative distribution function F(x)=P(Xi​≤x). Then F describes the sampling law, while Fn​ varies across repeated statistical samples. The value F5​(1)=0.4 is an observed fraction and an estimate of F(1); it does not establish that the population probability is 0.4. Even when F is continuous, every finite Fn​ is discrete.
For any threshold x fixed before sampling, the indicator functions are independent Bernoulli random variables with success probability F(x). Therefore the count has a binomial distribution and
nFn​(x)∼Binomial(n,F(x)),E[Fn​(x)]=F(x),Var(Fn​(x))=nF(x)(1−F(x))​.
(25)
The expected value follows by adding the expected values of the indicator functions; the variance follows by adding their variances using independence and dividing by n2. Thus Fn​(x) is an unbiased estimator of F(x) at a fixed threshold. Controlling the error at every threshold at once requires more than a fixed-threshold calculation: the DKW inequality supplies such control, and the Glivenko-Cantelli theorem describes its uniform convergence almost surely as n grows.
Comparing Fn​ with a proposed cumulative distribution function also motivates goodness-of-fit tests, including the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson–Darling test, and the Cramér–von Mises criterion. A standard Kolmogorov-Smirnov test calibration assumes a fully specified continuous population law; fitting its statistical parameters from the same statistical sample changes that calibration.[ref]

Simultaneous empirical distribution confidence band ([Ln​(x),Un​(x)])

Words: 426
Empirical distribution function OurBigBook.com
Fix a failure probability 0<α<1 and assume an independent and identically distributed statistical sample. A finite-sample confidence band for its population cumulative distribution function is
εn,α​=2nlog(2/α)​​,Ln​(x)=max{0,Fn​(x)−εn,α​},Un​(x)=min{1,Fn​(x)+εn,α​}.
(27)
Here log is the natural logarithm. The DKW inequality implies
P(Ln​(x)≤F(x)≤Un​(x) for every x∈R)≥1−α.
(28)
This is simultaneous coverage over the whole real line, valid at each fixed sample size.[ref]
To obtain the band, solve 2e−2nε2=α for the positive ε. Outside a failure event of probability at most α, ∣Fn​(x)−F(x)∣≤εn,α​ for every x. Since a cumulative distribution function already lies in [0,1], clipping the endpoints to this interval preserves the coverage event. The guarantee is at least 1−α, and need not equal it.
Choose α=0.1, giving at least 90% simultaneous coverage under the stated model. For n=5,50,500, respectively, the half-widths before clipping are
ε5,0.1​≈0.54733,ε50,0.1​≈0.17308,ε500,0.1​≈0.054733.
(29)
For the chosen five observations, the band at x=1 is [0,0.94733], while at x=4 it is approximately [0.25267,1]. At x=3 the unclipped band would be [0.05267,1.14733], so clipping gives [0.05267,1]. The broad uncertainty is informative: five observations give a precise description of themselves, but a coarse bound for an unknown population cumulative distribution function.
A collection of 90% pointwise confidence intervals only promises coverage separately at each preselected threshold; it does not promise 90% coverage of an entire cumulative distribution function. Here the one simultaneous event permits inspecting any threshold after seeing the data. The probability refers to repeated sampling of the entire statistical sample, with F fixed. It does not assign 90% probability to a fixed F after observing this particular band, and it is not a prediction interval for a future observation. The displayed n=5,50,500 comparison gives a guarantee for each fixed n separately, not simultaneous validity over all sample sizes or an optional stopping rule. The chosen observations are an illustration; the coverage claim follows from the DKW inequality, not from their appearance or a simulation. Dependence or observations with different sampling laws require another argument.
At fixed α, multiplying n by 100 divides the half-width by 10. Conversely, a desired half-width δ>0 is ensured by n≥log(2/α)/(2δ2), rounded up to an integer. For α=0.1 and δ=0.1, this sufficient sample size is 150. This makes the confidence band useful for planning how many observations are needed before estimating threshold probabilities to a chosen simultaneous accuracy.

Sample median (Xn​)

Words: 228 Articles: 1
Median OurBigBook.com
The sample median is a central value of an ordered statistical sample. The usual numerical convention selects the middle order statistic for odd sample size and the arithmetic mean of the two central order statistics for even sample size:
Xn​={X(m+1)​,(X(m)​+X(m+1)​)/2,​n=2m+1,n=2m.​
(58)
NIST uses this convention. [ref]. For (0.7,0.1,0.9,0.4,0.2), the sample median is 0.4; for (0.1,0.2,0.4,0.7), it is (0.2+0.4)/2=0.3, which need not be an observed value.
More generally, every value between the two central order statistics in an even statistical sample is a median of its empirical distribution function. The generalized-inverse sample quantile at p=1/2 selects the lower central order statistic in that case, so it can differ from the midpoint convention. Ties are allowed in all these definitions.
The sample median measures the center using sorted positions. Changing the largest observation from 0.9 to 9 in the five-value example leaves the sample median at 0.4, while the sample mean rises from 0.46 to 2.08. Its sampling distribution still depends on the population probability distribution: the mean 1/2 found for five observations from a uniform distribution is a special calculation, and a sample median's expected value need not equal the population median in general.
For a concrete counterexample, three independent and identically distributed random variables with rate-one exponential distribution have sample median X(2)​ with expected value 1/3+1/2=5/6, by independent exponential order-statistic spacings. The population median instead solves 1−e−m=1/2, giving m=log2≈0.693147. Thus even the middle order statistic can have mean different from the population median.

Normal distribution (N(μ,σ2))

Words: 2k Articles: 37
Probability distribution OurBigBook.com
The normal distribution is a probability distribution on the real line with mean μ and positive standard deviation σ. Its probability density function is
fX​(x)=σ2π​1​exp(−2σ2(x−μ)2​),x∈R,σ>0.
(67)
In the notation X∼N(μ,σ2), the second parameter is the variance σ2, not the standard deviation σ. The probability density function is symmetric about μ, highest there, and integrates to one. These formulas and the parameter convention are given in MIT 18.05, Reading 5c, §5: normal distributions.
The normal distribution is a location-scale family: if Z is a standard normal random variable, then X=μ+σZ. Changing μ moves the center; changing σ stretches the horizontal distances from it. The reciprocal factor 1/σ lowers the probability density function as the curve widens, preserving total area. This is why one standard normal distribution suffices to calculate probabilities for the whole family. [ref].
The height fX​(x) is a probability density function value, not P(X=x). For a≤b, the probability P(a≤X≤b)=∫ab​fX​(x)dx is an area, and P(X=x)=0 for every individual x. If X is measured in some unit, μ and σ use that unit, σ2 uses its square, and fX​ uses its reciprocal; the integral is a dimensionless quantity. A change of measurement unit therefore changes the height without changing the probability. The area interpretation is developed in MIT 18.05, Reading 5b: continuous random variables.
The usefulness of the normal distribution goes beyond its simple shape. Under the central limit theorem, sums of independent and identically distributed random variables with finite positive variance, after centering and scaling, approach the standard normal distribution. Thus approximations by a normal distribution can arise even when the individual random variables have quite different probability distributions. The hypotheses matter: a model of measurement error still needs evidence that this approximation is appropriate. [ref]. Exact closure under a linear combination of independent normal random variables provides another reason the family is convenient.
Historically, the curve appeared in a different problem from fitting measurements. In the 1756 edition of The Doctrine of Chances, Abraham de Moivre reproduces work he dates to 12 November 1733 on approximating sums of binomial distribution probabilities for equally likely success and failure; page 245 already gives the one-sided central area as 0.341344. [ref]. In his 1809 Theoria motus, Carl Friedrich Gauss derived a normal distribution for measurement error from a condition on the arithmetic mean, then connected maximizing its likelihood to minimizing the sum of squared errors under that model, the principle behind ordinary least squares. These are distinct contributions: approximating binomial distribution probabilities and justifying an estimation rule. [ref].
For a short normalization check, substitute z=(x−μ)/σ in the integral of fX​. The Gaussian integral gives ∫R​e−z2/2dz=2π​, so the total area is one. The standard normal density is an even function, giving E[Z]=0; integration by parts gives E[Z2]=1. Then linearity of expectation and the variance scaling rule applied to X=μ+σZ yield mean μ and variance σ2.

Multivariate Gaussian distribution OurBigBook.com
For centered jointly Gaussian random variables, an odd product has zero expectation, and an even product's expectation is the sum over all pairings of the products of the pair covariances. In particular,
E[X1​X2​X3​X4​]=E[X1​X2​]E[X3​X4​]+E[X1​X3​]E[X2​X4​]+E[X1​X4​]E[X2​X3​].
(69)
For a proof, the moment-generating function is exp(tTΣt/2). Differentiating once in each variable at zero leaves precisely products of covariance entries indexed by complete pairings. No independence assumption between the coordinates is needed.
Gaussian even-moment pairing count (EX2n=(2n−1)!!vn)
Words: 54
Isserlis's theorem OurBigBook.com
For a centered scalar normal random variable of variance v, the Isserlis theorem sums complete pairings of 2n factors. The first factor has 2n−1 partners, then 2n−3 choices remain for the first unpaired factor, giving (2n−1)!!=(2n)!/(2nn!). Odd moments vanish. Summing the moment-generating function gives exp(vs2/2). This is a scalar formula, not a formula for the length of a vector.

For the standard normal density ϕ and distribution function Φ, the upper-tail Mills ratio is (1−Φ(x))/ϕ(x). Ratios involving a Gaussian density and tail probability control truncated-normal moments and Gaussian-tail asymptotics.

Two successive integrations by parts of the standard normal density tail give positive remainder integrals establishing these strict inequalities for every x>0. The lower bound can be negative at small x without invalidating the inequality.

Gaussian random variable (X∼N(μ,σ2))

Words: 338 Articles: 4
Normal distribution OurBigBook.com
A Gaussian random variable is a random variable whose probability distribution is a normal distribution. For σ>0, write X=μ+σZ with a standard normal random variable Z; conversely, standardization of a normal random variable recovers Z=(X−μ)/σ. For example, X∼N(100,152) has mean 100, standard deviation 15, and variance 225. The outcome x=115 corresponds to standard score z=1, one standard deviation above the mean.
Some definitions also allow a Gaussian random variable with σ=0. This means X=μ almost surely, with variance zero and probability distribution equal to the Dirac measure δμ​. It has no probability density function with respect to Lebesgue measure: P(X=μ)=1. The positive-scale density formula and division by σ apply only when σ>0. MIT's constructive definition explicitly includes the constant case. [ref].

Gaussian series with square-summable coefficients (∑j​αj​Xj​∼N(0,∑j​αj2​))

Words: 199 Articles: 2
Gaussian random variable OurBigBook.com
For independent standard Gaussian Xj​ and ∑αj2​<∞, the partial sums are Cauchy in L2 space, since a tail's squared norm is the corresponding sum of coefficient squares. Completeness gives an L2 limit. The finite-sum characteristic functions converge to exp[−t2∑αj2​/2], identifying the limit as Gaussian, including the zero-variance case. The identification needs convergence of distributions, not just agreement of the first two moments.
Almost sure convergence criterion for an independent Gaussian series (∑k​ak​Zk​ converges a.s.⟺∑k​ak2​<∞)
Words: 136 Articles: 1
Gaussian series with square-summable coefficients OurBigBook.com
For independent standard Gaussian random variables, the partial sums have characteristic functions exp(−u2vn​/2), where vn​=∑k≤n​ak2​. A finite almost-sure limit implies convergence of these characteristic functions to one continuous at zero; vn​→∞ would instead give zero at every nonzero u. Conversely, bounded vn​ makes the partial sums an martingale bounded in L2 space, which converges almost surely and in L2 space.
Threshold stopping of an independent Gaussian series (EMT​=0⟺∑k​ak2​<∞)
Words: 84
Almost sure convergence criterion for an independent Gaussian series OurBigBook.com
Let Mn​=∑k≤n​ak​Zk​, and stop on first reaching a fixed positive threshold. If the coefficient squares are summable, uniform integrability gives the stopped mean zero, with the terminal limit used on T=∞. If the coefficient squares diverge, P(Mn​≥R)→1/2 for each fixed R. Thus P(supn​Mn​=∞)≥1/2. This event is unaffected by changing finitely many of the independent variables, so the Kolmogorov zero-one law makes its probability one. Hence T<∞ and MT​ is at least the positive threshold; its expectation, finite or infinite, cannot be zero.

Half-normal distribution (H=∣Z∣)

Words: 208 Articles: 1
Normal distribution OurBigBook.com
The half-normal distribution describes the absolute value of a centered Gaussian random variable. Its unit-scale version is H=∣Z∣ for a standard normal random variable Z. It folds the negative half of the standard normal distribution onto the positive half, retaining the size of a deviation while discarding its sign. If a centered Gaussian random variable models measurement error, its magnitude therefore has a half-normal distribution.
fH​(x)=⎩⎨⎧​2ϕ(x)=π2​​e−x2/2,0,​x≥0,x<0,​FH​(x)={2Φ(x)−1,0,​x≥0,x<0.​
(71)
Here ϕ is the standard normal density and Φ is the standard normal distribution function. For x≥0, the event H≤x is −x≤Z≤x, so the symmetric probability distribution of Z gives FH​(x)=Φ(x)−Φ(−x)=2Φ(x)−1. The upper-tail probability is therefore P(H>x)=2(1−Φ(x)). For example, P(H≤1)≈0.6826894921. The doubled probability density function integrates to one on [0,∞), and P(H=0)=0.
The mean and variance of the unit-scale half-normal distribution are
E[H]=π2​​,Var(H)=1−π2​.
(72)
For a short derivation, E[H]=2∫0∞​xϕ(x)dx=2ϕ(0) because ϕ′(x)=−xϕ(x), while H2=Z2 gives E[H2]=1. More generally, σ∣Z∣ for σ>0 has a half-normal distribution with probability density function 2ϕ(x/σ)/σ for x≥0. Its mean is σ2/π​ and its variance is σ2(1−2/π); here σ is the scale of the underlying Gaussian random variable, not the standard deviation of its absolute value.

The underlying radial symmetry makes radius and angle independent.

Normal distribution OurBigBook.com
The standard normal distribution is N(0,1): the normal distribution with mean zero, variance one and standard deviation one. Its standard normal density ϕ integrates to one; its standard normal distribution function Φ records the area accumulated from −∞ to a threshold. The distinction matters: ϕ(0)=1/2π​≈0.398942, Φ(0)=1/2, and P(Z=0)=0 for a standard normal random variable Z.
For a toy measurement X∼N(100,152), leave the measurement unit unspecified. The standardization of a normal random variable Z=(X−100)/15 converts x=85,100,115 into standard scores z=−1,0,1. Using the standard normal distribution function,

(75)
